alan_look_rafa_bed: The mattress. My clothes all over the floor, in a way that tells the whole story without anybody needing to tell it.
alan_look_studio_window: The cathedral's two black towers, and a grey sky. Santa Ana's bells have stopped. I haven't.

alan_s_rafa_1: No. I know the man he works for.
alan_s_truth: Rafa. Last night. When you asked me if there was someone.
alan_s_truth_2: There is. His name's Vasco. Eight months. He's up on the mountain at Artenara, on the dig. Yeray's dig.
alan_s_truth_3: And I lied to you. You asked me straight, and you deserved a straight answer. I'm sorry.
rafa_s_truth_2: You said no. [pause] Nobody says no like that unless it's yes.

alan_look_bed_sat: Unmade on Vasco's side, from yesterday morning. His jacket on the chair, shoulders squared. His watch, forgotten.

alan_call_sat_3: I can't reach him. He's on the mountain. The radio's off.
ines_call_sat_4: Then find a way. You've always been very good at finding ways into places you shouldn't be. Find a way into one you should.
alan_read_fax_1: 'It comes for every soul that was taken back from it.' [pause] Pepe. Doña Pino. [pause] 'It strikes first at whoever understands the lock.' Elena understood it.

vasco_v_02: Most Portuguese men are sad. It's the national sport.
yeray_v_04: They're not going to Las Palmas.

vasco_offpath_1: It's off. [pause] The beam is off its path.

vasco_sanjuan_2: Dead centre of the great triangle. The biggest of them all. [pause] And the seventh disc, the last in the line, decides it.

baute_v_01: You've solved it. I knew you would.

narr_s_wake_1: He wakes because the bells of Santa Ana are ringing for eight o'clock. For a few seconds, eyes still closed, he doesn't know where he is, and he is happy.
narr_s_wake_rafa: Rafa is at the gas ring in the corner, barefoot, in his shorts, humming. His back is brown and young, and there's charcoal on his shoulder blade in the shape of a thumbprint.
narr_s_wake_drawing: And propped against the wall at the foot of the mattress, where Alan would see it the moment he woke, is a sheet of heavy paper with a drawing on it.
narr_s_drawing_1: It's Alan, asleep. Charcoal, quick and soft, a few dozen lines. One hand under his cheek, his mouth a little open, his face completely unguarded. Younger than it has any right to be.
narr_s_drawing_2: It's the most beautiful drawing anyone has ever made of him. He looks at it, and he feels sick.
narr_s_dress: He finds his clothes on the floor and puts them on. The cream linen suit smells of rum and turpentine and someone else's skin.
narr_s_go: He should go now, before Rafa turns round. Leave the money on the counter and go, and be someone else by lunchtime. That's what he has always done.
narr_s_window: He stands at the window with his hands on the sill, looking at the cathedral's two black towers and the grey sky, and makes himself think it, in words, all the way to the end.
alan_s_window_1: I lied to him. He asked me, straight out, and I lied.
alan_s_window_2: And Vasco said two things. Only two. Tell me first. Never to settle a fight.
alan_s_window_3: I broke both of them in one night. [pause] And the second one I broke on purpose.
narr_s_sketch_1: He reads it three times. Then he sits down, slowly, on the edge of the table among the brushes, and puts the napkin down very carefully, as if it might go off.
alan_s_sketch_1: Not Montesdeoca. Not the van, not the hotel, not the circled resorts on the map.
alan_s_sketch_2: Baute. [pause] Every night, one by one, down into a vault under the mountain. Only he has the key. And Vasco signed the transfer sheets himself.
alan_s_sketch_3: He's up there now. With Baute. Through to Monday. Calling him Rayco.
alan_s_sketch_4: I heard every word of it last night. I was too busy watching Rafa's hands to listen.
narr_s_coffee: He makes it in an old aluminium pot, yawning. They drink it at the table by the window. It's very good coffee.
narr_s_napkin: On the table between them the sketchbook lies open, a paper napkin from the bar tucked into it like a bookmark. Alan looks at it without meaning to.
narr_s_rafa_sees: Rafa sees his face, and sees the napkin, and sees where Alan's eyes keep going.
rafa_s_yeray_1: Yeray. Pobre. He talks when he drinks. I write it down.
rafa_s_yeray_2: It's a bad habit. I'll stop one day. [pause] You know him?
alan_s_ask_yeray: What else did he say? Yeray.
rafa_s_yeray_more: That his professor is a great man. He said it six times.
rafa_s_yeray_more_2: Nobody says it six times about a great man, hombre.
rafa_s_drawn: At dawn. The light was good and you weren't talking.
rafa_s_drawn_2: You sleep like a man who's been let off something.
rafa_s_later: Drink. I'm not going anywhere. It's my flat.
alan_s_truth_4: We had a fight yesterday morning, and he left. And I came out last night to be someone who didn't have anything to lose.
narr_s_truth_2: Rafa looks at him for a long moment. Then he looks down at his coffee.
narr_s_truth_3: He smiles, a little, but it's a different smile from last night's. Older.
rafa_s_truth_3: I'm twenty-three, Alan. I'm not stupid. I just thought, he's sad, and he's beautiful, and he's leaving on Sunday anyway.
rafa_s_truth_5: [pause] It matters. I know it matters. I'm sorry too.
narr_s_truth_4: They sit there in the grey light.
narr_s_truth_5: Then Rafa gets up and fetches the drawing from the foot of the mattress. He blows on it, gently, to lift off the loose dust, and holds it out.
rafa_s_drawing_2: Take it. It's yours. It's not mine. I just saw it.
rafa_s_drawing_3: It's the last time you'll look that young. You should have something to remember it by.
narr_s_walk_1: He walks back to the hotel through the Saturday morning streets, with the drawing rolled up under his arm and the napkin in his pocket.
narr_s_walk_2: The city is getting ready for its fiesta. Flags going up across the streets, strings of coloured bulbs, men unloading crates of beer on every corner.
narr_s_walk_3: In Triana a brass band practises in a doorway, badly. Posters everywhere: Fiestas Fundacionales. San Juan 1996. Five hundred and eighteen years.
narr_s_walk_4: Five hundred and eighteen years since the city was founded, on the twenty-fourth of June: the morning the sun turns back.
narr_s_walk_5: The beach is already full of families claiming their places for Sunday night. The tide is up the steps again. Nobody seems to notice.
narr_s_nieves_1: Nieves is behind the desk. She looks at him as he comes in: at the suit, and the hour, and the roll of paper under his arm, and his face.
narr_s_nieves_2: Her eyebrow doesn't move at all. That's how he knows how bad he looks.
alan_s_msg_2: From Dr. Teles? From the dig?
narr_s_pigeon: Nieves looks at the pigeonhole for 404. It's empty. She looks at it slightly longer than she needs to, as if something might appear in it, for his sake.
nieves_s_coffee: There's café in the machine. It's still terrible. I'll bring you some.
narr_s_room_1: The room is exactly as he left it, and exactly as Vasco left it the morning before. The bed unmade on one side. Vasco's good jacket on the chair. Vasco's watch on the bedside table, forgotten.
narr_s_room_2: And on the tiles by Vasco's side of the bed, a footprint.
narr_s_room_3: Wet. A man's bare foot, long and narrow, dark on the terracotta. Just one, pointing at the bed, as if someone had stepped out of the sea and stood there in the night, looking down at where Alan should have been sleeping.
alan_s_print_1: The balcony doors are shut. [pause] The bathroom's dry.
narr_s_room_4: He thinks, for no reason he can name, of his father. Pedro Sanches, who went out fishing off Cascais one morning when Alan was a boy, and never came back.
narr_s_room_5: Alan can't remember his face any more. Only a shape against a bright window.
narr_s_room_6: He kneels and touches the footprint. It's cold, and his fingertips come away tasting of salt.
narr_s_room_7: By the time Nieves knocks with the coffee, it has dried, and there is nothing there at all.
alan_s_call_due: Inês. [pause] The phone box. Before I lose my nerve.
ines_call_sat_1b: The woman at the desk says you didn't come back last night. The woman at the desk sounds like a disappointed nun.
narr_call_sat_1: He stands with his forehead against the glass. Outside, Chano is serving a queue of people buying fireworks.
alan_call_sat_1b: And I went out, and I met someone. And I slept with him.
narr_call_sat_2: A long silence on the line from Lisbon.
ines_call_sat_2b: Alan, the rules. The two rules. He told me about them, in the shop, in January. He was so proud of himself for being modern.
ines_call_sat_2c: Tell me first. Never to settle a fight. [pause] So you broke both of them.
narr_call_sat_3: When she speaks again her voice is different. Not soft. She doesn't do soft. But steady.
ines_call_sat_5: And Alan. The letter from the cathedral. I've read it.
ines_call_sat_6: It took me two days, a dictionary of eighteenth-century abbreviations, and a professor of palaeography who thinks I'm in love with him.
ines_call_sat_7: It's from the founders. Three of them signed it. Your family. Bartolomeu Sanches is the first signature. [pause] Are you sitting down?
ines_call_sat_8: Then I'll read you the worst of it. The rest is on your hotel's fax machine. Read that sitting down.
ines_call_sat_9: A lock. That's their word, fechadura. The island's priestesses made it in fourteen eighty-three, to hold the Sea. With a capital S. The same Sea, Alan. The one from the cistern.
ines_call_sat_10: They called it up to drown the Castilian ships, and it came, and it didn't stop. And they shut it out again with the sun. With light. In a cave.
narr_call_sat_5: Alan's hand is tight on the receiver.
ines_call_sat_11: 'To shut the door again, one must stand in its water, at the door, at the first sunrise of the turning, and set the stones while it rises.'
ines_call_sat_12: 'The last of the priestesses did this. She set the stones, and the Sea withdrew. And it drew her down with it as it went, and she was not seen again.'
ines_call_sat_14: And a line at the end, underlined, in another hand. 'If the door is opened in your time, the Sea will strike first at any who understand the lock. And at our blood above all, for it knows the hands that bound it once.'
ines_call_sat_15: 'And it will come for every soul it once had in its grip and lost. If one must stand in the water, pray God it is not you.'
ines_call_sat_16: Alan. The cistern backed away from you because of whose blood you are. In Lisbon that saved you. Here, with the door opening, it's the reason it'll want you first.
ines_call_sat_17: So if it's opened in your time—
narr_call_sat_7: The pips. The money's running out.
ines_call_sat_18: Tell him today. Tell him everything. And then come home. Promise me. Promise me you'll come h—
narr_s_chano_1: Chano has a newspaper for him, and a face.
narr_s_chano_2: He turns the paper round on the counter. A short column on page six: a former lifeguard, found dead at home. Agustín Ramos, seventy-one. Natural causes.
chano_s_2: My cousin's husband knew him. Forty years on the playa. Two hundred people he pulled out. Two hundred.
chano_s_3: And he drowns in his armchair, in front of the television.
chano_s_4: They say heart. Heart, with seawater in his lungs. That's two this week. Pepe, and now Agustín.
alan_s_chano_1: Did he ever nearly drown? Agustín. When he was young?
chano_s_5: Fifty-eight. In a rip. Everybody knows that story. It's why he became a lifeguard.
narr_s_chano_3: Alan doesn't answer. He's looking at the beach: at the tide on the steps, and the families laying out their towels round the bonfires for tomorrow night.
alan_s_chano_2: Taken back. [pause] The hotel. Inês's fax.
narr_s_tried_1: He tries. Later, he will need to know that he tried.
narr_s_tried_2: The museum is closed for the weekend. When he hammers on the door, the guard comes and looks at him through the glass, and shakes his head.
narr_s_tried_3: Alan asks him to radio the dig. The guard tries. No answer. He tries again. No answer.
narr_s_tried_4: Every car on the island is booked for San Juan. The woman at the car-hire desk in Triana laughs at him, not unkindly.
narr_s_tried_5: The bus to Artenara goes once a day, at seven in the morning. It has gone.
alan_s_tried: Fifty kilometres. Uphill. Through the cloud.
narr_s_tried_6: He'll take the bus in the morning. Seven o'clock. At the dig by ten. He'll find Vasco and tell him everything, and they'll deal with Baute together.
narr_s_tried_7: It's the most reasonable decision he has made all week, and he hates it.
narr_s_seven: At seven in the evening, people run past the hotel doors, shouting. Towards La Isleta.
narr_flood_2: It comes up through the drains and the cracks between the cobbles, quietly, steadily, black and cold. Ankle deep, then shin deep, in the low streets where Pepe Santana lived.
narr_flood_3: Old women stand in their doorways sweeping it back with brooms, and it comes in round the brooms. Men carry televisions up the stairs. A child is crying.
narr_flood_4: A dog swims past, paddling furiously, with an expression of enormous offence.
narr_flood_5: And under the grey panza, low on the water, the black mist lies over the harbour like smoke over a battlefield.
narr_flood_door: Doña Pino's door is open, the water over the step. Inside, by a candle, Don Lolo sits on a kitchen chair with his trousers rolled to the knee and his feet in the black water, mending a net in his lap.
narr_flood_bed: Behind him, on a narrow bed, Doña Pino. Soaked. Coughing up water, salt water, onto the pillow. But alive, propped on her elbows, and glaring.
pino_s_1b: I sat down to say a rosary and I fell asleep, and I woke up drowning in my own bed.
pino_s_2: He doesn't sleep. Fifty-five years married, and he has never once slept through the night. I always said it would kill me.
pino_s_3: It saved me. He heard the sea in the room. He pulled me up by my hair.
narr_flood_lolo: Don Lolo looks up at Alan. He takes the cigarette out of the corner of his mouth, looks at it, and puts it back.
lolo_s_3: Fifty-five years, señor. And she still hasn't forgiven me for the first one.
narr_flood_lolo_2: It's the first full sentence Alan has ever heard him speak.
narr_flood_later: Later, the water begins, slowly, impossibly, to sink back into the drains it came from. The neighbours come with towels and soup and opinions.
narr_flood_later_2: Doña Pino, in dry clothes, refuses the hospital in terms that turn a young doctor red to the ears.
narr_flood_missal: Alan sits by her. She has her missal on her knee, open at the inside cover. Two names crossed out. Two not.
pino_s_know: Sí. [pause] You know a lot about what the sea does, Portuguese.
alan_s_coming: It's coming for me too. Not for the same reason. But it's coming.
narr_flood_told: He tells her. Not all of it. The cistern. The black water at his chest. The thing in the dark that looked at him, and knew his blood, and backed away. The bells. His family.
narr_flood_pen: When he has finished she is quiet a long time. Then she unscrews an old fountain pen and holds it out to him, with the missal, open at the names.
narr_flood_name: At the bottom of the list, under her name, Alan writes his own. His hand is perfectly steady.
pino_s_name_2: Go home, Portuguese. Go to bed. Say your prayers.
narr_s_night_1: He goes back to the hotel and lies down in his clothes, on his own side of the bed, facing Vasco's: Vasco's watch, and the place on the tiles where the footprint was.
narr_s_night_2: He puts the rolled-up drawing on the pillow beside him. The phone on the bedside table does not ring.
narr_s_night_3: The sea comes in through the balcony doors, and under it, closer every night, the other sound.
narr_s_night_4: On the desk by the door, his plane ticket. Lisbon, via Madrid. Sunday, eleven fifteen.
narr_s_night_5: Tomorrow there will be two things to choose between: a bus at seven that goes up the mountain, and a plane at eleven fifteen that goes home. One of them might save his life.
narr_s_night_6: He doesn't know which. He lies awake and stares at the phone, and it doesn't ring.
narr_v_camp_1: Vasco Teles hasn't slept since Thursday. At seven on Saturday morning he's standing on the edge of a cliff above the clouds, trying very hard not to think about Alan.
narr_v_camp_2: The panza de burro lies under him like a frozen sea, flat and white to the horizon, filling the valleys, swallowing the coast. Far to the west, Teide stands up out of it like another island.
narr_v_camp_3: And over it all, the sun. Blazing, enormous, with nothing between it and him.
narr_v_camp_4: Down there, under the cloud, it's grey. Down there, Alan is asleep in a hotel room, or not asleep. Down there is the sea.
vasco_look_radio_1: I could call the museum. The museum could call the hotel. In ten minutes I could be hearing his voice.
narr_v_radio: He looks at the little dead dial, and feels something like relief, and is ashamed of the relief. He doesn't touch it.
narr_v_charts_1: Dr. Elena Suárez, the sacred-light specialist before him. Rayco mentioned her once, on the first day, with a strange flat look: an accident in December, on the mountain road. Then he changed the subject.
narr_v_charts_2: Her drawings are beautiful. Sun-path charts of Cave 6 in fine black pen, every triangle numbered, and over them in red the beam's track, hour by hour, for every day of the year that matters.
narr_v_charts_3: On the last chart, the summer solstice, the beam in red as usual. And beside it, in pencil, a second track. It goes somewhere else. It doesn't touch the triangles at all.
narr_v_charts_4: In the margin, in a hand no longer small or patient, one word, underlined three times. Puerta. Door.
narr_v_yeray_1: Yeray pours it into a tin mug and hands it over without meeting his eyes. They stand side by side at the edge of the camp and look at the cloud.
yeray_v_02b: You should go. Everyone goes. [pause] There was a Portuguese guy there.
yeray_v_02c: Funny. Making Rafa laugh. Making everyone laugh.
yeray_v_02d: Sad, though. Underneath. Like a man at his own fiesta who doesn't know why he came.
narr_v_yeray_3: There are a great many Portuguese men in the world. There are probably several in Las Palmas on any given night.
narr_v_yeray_4: Yeray laughs, briefly, and winces at the noise. Then he gathers himself, the way a man does before jumping into cold water.
yeray_v_03b: Dr. Baute says they're going down to Las Palmas. To the museo. For conservation.
narr_v_yeray_5: Yeray looks at him then, straight in the face, for the first time. The boy isn't hungover. He's frightened.
narr_v_yeray_6: Yeray throws the rest of his coffee out over the edge, in a brown arc that vanishes into the white.
yeray_v_04b: Forget it. I'm hungover. I talk rubbish.
narr_v_yeray_7: Vasco stands at the edge of the cliff with his tin mug. A Portuguese man in Rafa's bar. Funny. Sad underneath.
narr_v_cave_1: Cave 6 is a hundred metres along the cliff, by a path cut into the rock, with a rope on iron pins for a handrail. A small square doorway, barely higher than a man. You have to stoop to go in.
narr_v_cave_2: And then you straighten up, and you're inside a dome. Six metres across, carved by hand out of soft rock, pale and gold, and every centimetre of it engraved with triangles.
narr_v_cave_3: Hundreds of them, large and small, some deep and sharp, some worn almost to nothing. Every one of them points down.
narr_v_cave_4: High in the dome a narrow slot opens to the sky. A blade of sunlight comes through it, thin and white as a knife, and lies against the wall on bare rock between the triangles.
narr_v_cave_5: Vasco stands in the middle of the cave and feels, as he has every morning for eight days, his heart turn over.
vasco_look_sockets_1: Seven sockets along the lip of the channel. Five empty. Two still holding their discs.
vasco_look_sockets_2: [pause] I never counted them, the first day. I was looking at the light.
narr_v_offpath_1: He lays Elena's solstice chart against the wall. Her red line runs through the triangles, across the largest cluster, all the way to the great triangle at the back.
narr_v_offpath_2: His chalk marks don't follow it. A few centimetres off at first, then more, the gap widening with the hours. By eleven the beam is falling on bare stone, as if it were lost.
narr_v_steer_1: He climbs the ladder to the two discs that are left and, very carefully, with his fingertips, turns one. It moves stiffly, with a faint gritty sound: stone on glass.
narr_v_steer_2: And across the cave the blade of light jumps. It slides sideways, all at once, and lands squarely on a triangle, so that every cut line of it stands out in gold and black.
vasco_steer_3: And with five of them gone, the light falls wherever it likes.
narr_v_sanjuan_1: He sits on the floor with Elena's charts spread round him and works it out: her measurements of the channel, his of the sun, and a great deal of trigonometry he hasn't done since school, rebuilt on the backs of her charts.
vasco_sanjuan_1b: The beam comes in, goes from mirror to mirror down the slot, crosses the cave, and lands...
narr_v_angle_1: The angle the seventh disc has to hold is very particular. He works it out three times, to be sure.
narr_v_angle_2: Then he sits back against the wall and laughs: a short, startled laugh, alone in the cave, echoing up into the dome.
narr_v_angle_3: The tilt of the Earth. The latitude of the Tropic of Cancer, where the sun stands still before it turns. The number every schoolchild learns and forgets.
narr_v_angle_4: And because he is thorough, and because Elena drew a second line, he works out the other number: where the beam would fall with the seventh disc turned another way. On the floor, at the foot of the great triangle, where all the arrows point.
narr_v_angle_5: He gets that number too, and looks at it for a long time. Then he tears the corner off the chart, folds it very small, puts it in his mouth, and swallows it.
narr_v_angle_6: The way the old priests in the Patriarchate's archives did with things that should never have been written down. It's in his head now. Nowhere else.
narr_v_whole: He stands up and looks at the cave the way he was trained to look at a church when he first walks in. Not the details. The shape. What the building is for.
vasco_v_arrows: The triangles. Arrows, every one, pointing down. At the rock, at the mountain. And under the mountain, a thousand metres down, at the sea.
vasco_v_read: And the light walks across them every day, spring to autumn, like a finger on a line of text. Someone reading a sentence aloud, over and over, to keep it true.
vasco_v_read_2: And the discs hold the light in place. So it never misses a word.
narr_v_alan_1: And then, before he can stop himself, the next thing.
narr_v_alan_2: The mist on the promenade. The thing Alan told him on Friday morning, in the grey light, too fast and in the wrong order: the thing Vasco was too angry to hear.
narr_v_alan_3: The sea coming up the steps. The old fisherman drowned in his bed. It's here. The thing from the cistern. It's here.
vasco_v_alan_2: And I said, you could have just asked me. [pause] I said, go home.
narr_v_out: He goes out of the cave so fast he cracks his head on the low doorway, and doesn't feel it.
narr_v_fuse_1: He switches it on. Nothing. Off, and on again. The dial stays dead: no hum, no light.
narr_v_fuse_2: He kneels and opens the metal case. The neat rows of valves and wires, and the little glass holder where the fuse should be.
narr_v_fuse_3: Radios do not lose their fuses by themselves.
narr_v_fuse_4: He thinks of Yeray's face, frightened. Of the steel marks round the empty sockets. Of Elena's second line, and the word in the margin.
narr_v_fuse_5: Of Rayco's face on the first day, flat and strange: an accident in December, on the mountain road.
vasco_v_see: I haven't wanted to see this. I've walked past it every day for a week, because I didn't want to see it.
narr_v_shadow: A shadow falls across the radio.
narr_v_baute_1: Rayco Baute stands at the edge of the camp in his shirtsleeves and his faded field hat, against the blue sky and the white sea of cloud, a thermos in one hand and two tin mugs in the other.
narr_v_baute_2: He's smiling at Vasco with enormous affection, and enormous sadness, the way a father smiles at a son who has just found out something about him.
